extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in hacking/security, security technologists, privacy advocates, and general readers of Little Brother
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and prescriptive rules about how to think about, analyze, and publish on security (security mindset, disclosure, threat modelling), together with the full legal terms and conditions of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0 Unported license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security is a mindset
rubrics_metrics.description: Security is a way of thinking: constantly looking for ways a security system fails; analyze threats, failure modes, and exploitation paths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend time looking at real-world security systems (cameras, restaurants, airport security, bank teller procedures, traffic lights, locks) to understand what threats they protect against and what they don't. Thinking this way will reveal wasted resources and weak security controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designers cannot adequately analyze their own designs
rubrics_metrics.description: No one is qualified to analyze their own security designs because designer and analyzer are the same person with the same limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Security designs must be analyzed by others (independent reviewers) because systems must be secure against threats the designers didn't think of; incorporate third-party review and adversarial testing into the design lifecycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish vulnerabilities — secrecy is weak security
rubrics_metrics.description: Only bad security relies on secrecy; good security works even if all details are public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing vulnerabilities forces designers to improve systems and helps consumers choose better security products. Secrecy and security are not the same; openness improves security over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and use threat modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Figure out how systems work, what threats they protect against and what threats they don't, and how they can be exploited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When examining a system, explicitly identify its threat model and test for threats outside it. Use concrete experiments (e.g., gait-recognition vs rocks in shoes) to validate assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy as essential to security
rubrics_metrics.description: Privacy should be understood as essential to security, not oppositionally; trading privacy for security is misguided unless it yields real security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate security measures by whether they actually increase safety for intended threats and weigh privacy costs; avoid security theater that only heightens fear without real protective value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical experimentation and publication
rubrics_metrics.description: If you find a novel way to break a security system, publish it so others can learn and designers can improve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing case studies and practical exploits (with responsible consideration of harm) benefits the broader community and consumer awareness; historical examples (bump key, Bic-pen Kryptonite) illustrate this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hackers' motivations and civic argument for hacking
rubrics_metrics.description: Hacking often stems from curiosity, ownership of hardware, and exploration rather than malice; society should tolerate and legitimize such inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize cultural and educational routes into hacking; encourage noncriminal exploration and oppose conflation of curious tinkering with terrorism or malicious intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid security theater and paranoia
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures that coerce people into ritualized procedures (e.g., stripping, daily shoe removal) without substantial threat mitigation are counterproductive and reinforce fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymaking should focus on effective threat mitigation rather than visible rituals that increase public fear and erode freedoms; preserve civil liberties while designing security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic action and freedom over reliance on systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom is preserved by civic courage and acting as a free society, not by building ever-more intrusive security systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for political engagement and civil liberties (e.g., join EFF, write to elected officials) rather than assuming technology alone will secure freedom.
